newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: GUATEMALA BLAMES UNRULY FANS FOR 80 SOCCER DEATHS.
newsitem.headline: GUATEMALA BLAMES UNRULY FANS FOR 80 SOCCER DEATHS.

text.p: The Guatemalan government blamed unruly fans on Thursday for a soccer stadium disaster that killed at least 80 people, but others said fake ticket sales flooded the arena with far too many spectators before the match began.

The victims were crushed in an avalanche of falling bodies at the Guatemalan stadium after fans without proper tickets charged in to see a World Cup soccer qualifying game between Costa Rica and Guatemala on Wednesday night, witnesses said.

The exact death toll from the tragedy was still unclear on Thursday. The municipal fire department estimated "82 or 83 dead," but Interior Minister Rodolfo Mendoza said the official death toll was 80 people, all Guatemalans, and 147 injured.
Either way, it was the worst stadium disaster in World Cup history.

President Alvaro Arzu held an emergency cabinet meeting to discuss the disaster and declared three days' national mourning. Public buildings were covered with black ribbons, flags flew at half mast and outdoor sports events were banned for two days.
Arzu cancelled a planned news conference without explanation but Mendoza showed up instead and fingered the crowd as the culprits for the tragedy.

"There was a brawl in the upper part of the stands at the south wing, which resulted in the people from above coming down on the people below and that brought about the tragedy," Mendoza told reporters.

Relatives and friends of the dead took a different view. "This is a tragedy that should have been prevented. It was corruption that let this happen because of all the forged tickets," said a grieving boy at the city morgue.

The boy, who refused to give his name, said he and his friends who died in the disaster had all been sold fake tickets by scalpers. His story was echoed by other relatives and local media, who all spoke of a flood of forged tickets circulating ahead of the game, filling the stadium far beyond capacity.
"Corruption Caused Tragedy," the afternoon daily La Hora said in a banner headline on Thursday.
Bodies of the dead were taken to a morgue near Guatemala City's main cemetery for relatives, mostly poor Indians, to identify.

Sad, resentful and angry by turns, the family members wept, sobbed and held on to each other as they filed in. Outside the building, 20 black hearses waited to carry away the cheap tin coffins for private burials starting Friday.

Jorge Mario Boche, the cousin of a victim, said: "The authorities are not capable of staging a soccer event like this. And they're not even capable of finding the people responsible for this terrible tragedy, either."
Capt. Julio Roberto Rodriguez, owner of the private company responsible for match security, admitted there was overcrowding and fake ticket sales but also blamed the crowd.
"There was a brawl caused by the people who were already inside," he said.

Guatemala's National Soccer Federation recognised there was a problem with fake tickets. "The fundamental cause was the sale of false tickets," Ferdi Berganza, manager of the national soccer team commission, told reporters.
"Shamefully, there were not enough people to be able to capture all the people (with) unauthorised tickets," Rodriguez admitted to reporters.
Mendoza said two men had been arrested before the match for selling fake tickets.

Guatemalan officials said the stadium was packed well beyond its 45,800 capacity an hour before kickoff, with some estimating that up to 60,000 were in the concrete 1940s facility close to Guatemala City's centre.

In a preliminary report submitted by a match commissioner who attended the game, FIFA, soccer's governing body in Switzerland, said angry fans kicked down an entrance door causing spectators inside to cascade down to the lower levels about half an hour before the game's scheduled start of 8 p.m. Wednesday (0200 GMT on Thursday).
But the owner of the private security company said: "At no time was the door broken down."

Rolando Pineda Lam, president of the National Soccer Federation, said he expected word from FIFA within 24 hours as to whether the international body would sanction the local federation or decertify the stadium for World Cup games.
